lessons.title: Docker and container images in depth
lessons.summary: What an image really is, how layers and the build cache work, multi-stage and distroless builds, containers versus VMs, and how to ship images that are small and secure.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A container image is a **packaged filesystem plus instructions for how to start a process from it**. A container is that process, running on a normal Linux kernel, with a restricted view of the machine: its own process tree, its own network stack, its own mount table, and limits on CPU and memory.

That is the whole trick. There is no "container kernel" and no emulated hardware. Docker (and containerd, Podman, and the OCI standards underneath them) are tooling around two kernel features, **namespaces** (what a process can see) and **cgroups** (what it can use), plus a clever way of shipping filesystems as stacked layers.

Why it matters in practice: the image you tested in CI is byte-for-byte the image that runs in production. "Works on my machine" turns into "works in this image digest", which is something you can reason about.

## What an image actually is
An OCI image has three parts:

- **Layers**: tarballs of filesystem changes. Each is identified by the SHA-256 of its content, so identical layers are stored and pulled once.
- **A config**: environment variables, the default user, working directory, entrypoint and command, exposed ports, and the ordered list of layer digests.
- **A manifest**: points at the config and layers. A multi-platform image adds an index that points at one manifest per architecture (for example `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`).

When you start a container, the runtime stacks the read-only layers with an overlay filesystem (usually `overlayfs`) and puts one thin **writable layer** on top. Writes go to that layer with copy-on-write; when the container is removed, that layer is gone. Anything you need to keep goes in a volume or, better, in an external service.

```text
container  [ writable layer (copy-on-write, deleted with the container) ]
image      [ layer 4: COPY dist/ /app            sha256:9f2c... ]
           [ layer 3: RUN npm ci --omit=dev       sha256:41ab... ]
           [ layer 2: COPY package*.json /app     sha256:0d77... ]
           [ layer 1: base image (debian + node)  sha256:c3e1... ]
```

Two consequences people miss:

1. **Layers are immutable.** If one instruction writes a file and a later one deletes it, the file is still in the image; the later layer only hides it. This is how secrets leak.
2. **Tags are mutable, digests are not.** `node:22` points at different bytes next month. `node:22@sha256:...` never changes.

## How the build cache works
Each instruction (`FROM`, `RUN`, `COPY`, `ADD`, and so on) produces a cache key from the instruction text, the parent layer, and for `COPY`/`ADD` a checksum of the files being copied. BuildKit walks the Dockerfile top to bottom; at the **first instruction whose key changed, the cache is invalidated for that step and every step after it**.

So the rule is: order instructions from least frequently changing to most frequently changing.

```dockerfile
# Bad: any source change reinstalls every dependency
COPY . .
RUN npm ci

# Good: the install layer is reused until package*.json changes
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
```

BuildKit adds two tools worth knowing:

- **Cache mounts** keep a package manager cache across builds without putting it in a layer: `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci`.
- **Remote cache** (`--cache-from` / `--cache-to`, for example `type=registry` or `type=gha` in GitHub Actions) lets CI runners, which start empty, reuse layers from previous builds.

And a `.dockerignore` file matters more than it looks: without it, `COPY . .` sends `node_modules`, `.git` and local `.env` files into the build context, slows every build, busts the cache on irrelevant changes and can leak secrets into the image.

## Multi-stage builds
Building needs compilers, dev dependencies, and source. Running needs only the output. A multi-stage build uses several `FROM` stages and copies just the artifacts into the final one.

A realistic Node.js service:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

FROM node:22-bookworm-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci

FROM deps AS build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs22-debian12:nonroot AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY --from=build /app/package.json ./
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["dist/server.js"]
```

What each choice buys:

- The `deps` stage is cached until the lockfile changes.
- `npm prune --omit=dev` strips test and build tooling before copying `node_modules`.
- The final stage has no npm, no compiler, no shell, no package manager. The distroless Node image's entrypoint is already `node`, so `CMD` is just the script path.
- The `:nonroot` tag runs as an unprivileged user by default.

The same pattern works for Go (build with `CGO_ENABLED=0`, copy one static binary into `distroless/static` or `scratch`), Java (build with Maven or Gradle, copy the JAR into a JRE-only image) and Python (build wheels in one stage, install them into a slim runtime).

## Base images: full, slim, Alpine, distroless
| Base | What is inside | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| `node:22` (Debian) | Full OS, compilers, many tools | Easy to debug, large, many CVEs to triage |
| `node:22-bookworm-slim` | Minimal Debian plus Node | Good default; still has a shell and apt |
| `node:22-alpine` | musl libc, BusyBox | Small, but musl differs from glibc; native modules and DNS behaviour can surprise you |
| distroless | Runtime and its libraries only, no shell | Smallest attack surface; debugging needs the `:debug` variant or ephemeral debug containers |
| `scratch` | Empty | Only for fully static binaries; you must add CA certificates and timezone data yourself |

The Google distroless README makes the argument plainly: what is not in the image cannot be exploited and does not show up in scanner reports. The cost is operational. You cannot `docker exec ... sh` into it, so you rely on logs, metrics, and tools like `kubectl debug` that attach a separate debugging container.

## Containers versus virtual machines
```text
        CONTAINERS                          VIRTUAL MACHINES
  [app A] [app B] [app C]              [app A]     [app B]
  [ libs ][ libs ][ libs ]             [guest OS]  [guest OS]
  ------- shared host kernel -------   [ hypervisor (KVM, Hyper-V) ]
  [        host hardware         ]     [      host hardware        ]
```

- **Isolation boundary.** A container is a process separated by namespaces (PID, network, mount, UTS, IPC, user, cgroup) and constrained by cgroups. A kernel bug is shared by every container on the host. A VM has its own kernel behind a hypervisor, which is a much smaller and better-tested boundary.
- **Startup and density.** Containers start in milliseconds to seconds and add almost no memory overhead. VMs boot a kernel and reserve memory.
- **Portability.** A Linux container needs a Linux kernel; Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows quietly runs a Linux VM for you.

The middle ground matters in interviews. **MicroVMs** such as Firecracker (the NSDI 2020 paper explains how AWS Lambda uses it) boot a minimal kernel in around a hundred milliseconds, giving VM isolation with near-container density. **gVisor** intercepts system calls in a user-space kernel. **Kata Containers** run each pod in a lightweight VM. Multi-tenant platforms that run untrusted code use these; a single company running its own services usually accepts plain containers.

## Image security, concretely
1. **Do not run as root.** Add `USER` (or use a `:nonroot` base). Root in a container is root on the host's kernel interface, limited only by namespaces and dropped capabilities. In Kubernetes, also set `runAsNonRoot: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` and drop all capabilities.
2. **Keep secrets out of layers and build args.** `ARG` and `ENV` values are visible in image history. Use BuildKit secret mounts:

```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci
```

```bash
docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc -t api:dev .
```

3. **Pin and update bases.** Pin by digest for reproducibility and let a bot (Renovate or Dependabot) open PRs when the base changes, so you get security fixes deliberately rather than never.
4. **Scan and generate an SBOM.** Tools such as Trivy, Grype or Docker Scout list known CVEs per package. Fail the build on fixable criticals, not on every low-severity finding, or people learn to ignore the scanner.
5. **Sign and verify.** Sign images in CI (Sigstore `cosign`, keyless via OIDC) and verify signatures at admission in the cluster. SLSA describes the provenance levels if the interviewer goes deeper into supply chain.

## Signals, PID 1 and graceful shutdown
Whatever your `CMD` starts is PID 1 inside the container. The kernel treats PID 1 specially: **signals with no handler installed are ignored**, rather than killing the process. Node.js does not install a SIGTERM handler by default. So `docker stop` (or Kubernetes deleting a pod) sends SIGTERM, nothing happens, and after the grace period (10 seconds for `docker stop`, 30 for Kubernetes by default) the process gets SIGKILL mid-request.

Fixes:

- Use the **exec form** `CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]`. The shell form `CMD node dist/server.js` runs `/bin/sh -c`, which becomes PID 1 and does not forward signals.
- Do not start production processes through `npm start`; run the runtime directly.
- Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close pools, exit.
- Use `docker run --init` or `tini` if the app spawns child processes that need reaping.

```ts
const server = app.listen(8080);
process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  server.close(async () => {
    await db.end();
    process.exit(0);
  });
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 25_000).unref();
});
```

## Trade-offs and when not to bother
- For a tiny internal tool, a slim base and a single stage is fine; distroless adds debugging friction.
- Alpine saves megabytes but can cost days when a native dependency behaves differently under musl. Prefer slim Debian or distroless unless you have measured a reason.
- Containers are not a security boundary for hostile code. If you run user-submitted code, use microVMs or gVisor.
- Do not containerise stateful databases on a laptop-style setup and call it production; managed databases or operators with real storage are a separate decision.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Huge images**: check `docker history <image>` and tools like `dive` to see which layer is big. Usual culprits: dev dependencies, build caches, `.git`, test fixtures.
- **Cache never hits in CI**: runners start clean; configure a registry or GitHub Actions cache backend.
- **"Works locally, crashes in prod"**: different architecture (an `arm64` laptop building an image for `amd64` servers). Build multi-platform with `docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64`.
- **Using `latest`**: you cannot tell what is running or roll back to it. Tag with the git SHA and deploy by digest.
- **Writing to the container filesystem**: logs and uploads vanish on restart. Log to stdout and stderr; store files in object storage.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you know containers are processes, not small VMs; whether you can write a cache-friendly, multi-stage Dockerfile; and whether you think about security and shutdown, which separates people who have operated containers from people who have only built them.

**A 60-second answer outline** for "how would you containerise this service?":
1. Multi-stage build: dependencies stage cached on the lockfile, build stage, minimal runtime stage.
2. Slim or distroless base pinned by digest, non-root user, no secrets in layers, `.dockerignore`.
3. Exec-form CMD, SIGTERM handling for graceful shutdown, logs to stdout.
4. CI builds once, tags with the git SHA, scans, signs, and pushes; deploys reference the digest.

**Follow-ups to expect:** Why is my image 1.5 GB? How do containers differ from VMs, and when is that difference a security problem? How do you debug a distroless container? How does Docker Desktop run Linux containers on a Mac?
keyPoints: An image is an ordered stack of read-only, content-addressed layers plus a config; a container adds one thin writable layer on top.
Build cache invalidates from the first changed instruction down, so copy dependency manifests and install before copying source.
Multi-stage builds keep compilers and dev dependencies out of the final image; distroless or slim bases shrink the attack surface further.
Containers share the host kernel and are isolated by namespaces and cgroups; VMs and microVMs give each workload its own kernel.
Run as non-root, keep secrets out of layers, pin base images by digest, scan and sign images, and make your process handle SIGTERM as PID 1.
interview: What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?
How do Docker image layers and the build cache work, and how do you write a Dockerfile that builds fast?
How would you make a production container image small and secure?
Your container takes 10 seconds to stop and drops in-flight requests on deploy. What is going on?

check.q: A Dockerfile does `COPY . .` and then `RUN npm ci`. Every code change reinstalls all dependencies. What is the fix?
options: Add `--no-cache` to the build
Copy package.json and the lockfile first, run `npm ci`, then copy the rest of the source
Switch the base image to Alpine
Move `npm ci` into the CMD instruction
check.why: The cache is invalidated from the first instruction whose inputs changed. Copying only the manifests before the install means the install layer is reused until dependencies actually change.

check.q: You delete a secret file in a later `RUN rm` instruction. Is the secret gone from the image?
options: Yes, the final filesystem no longer contains it
Yes, if the image is pushed with compression
No, it still exists in the earlier layer and anyone who pulls the image can extract it
check.why: Layers are immutable. Deleting a file adds a whiteout in a new layer but the earlier layer still ships with the image. Use BuildKit secret mounts so the secret never lands in a layer.

check.q: Why does a Node.js process started directly as PID 1 in a container often ignore `docker stop`?
options: PID 1 gets no default signal handlers, so SIGTERM is ignored unless the app installs a handler
Docker sends SIGKILL first
Node.js cannot receive signals inside namespaces
The container runtime blocks all signals to PID 1
check.why: The kernel does not apply default signal actions to PID 1 in a PID namespace. If the process does not handle SIGTERM, it keeps running until the runtime sends SIGKILL after the grace period.

lessons.title: Kubernetes for application engineers
lessons.summary: The reconciliation model, pods, Deployments, Services, Gateway API, config and secrets, probes, requests and limits, and the HPA, with the failure modes that bite in production.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Kubernetes is a **database of desired state plus a crowd of control loops**. You write objects ("I want 3 replicas of this image, reachable on port 80") to the API server, which stores them in etcd. Controllers watch those objects, compare them with reality, and act to close the gap. A node dies, pods vanish, the ReplicaSet controller notices fewer pods than desired and creates new ones; the scheduler places them; the kubelet on the chosen node starts them.

Nothing in Kubernetes is a one-shot command. Everything is **declarative and level-triggered**: controllers keep converging, so the system heals from partial failures without a human replaying steps. That is also why it can be confusing: when something is wrong you debug a loop, by reading object status and events, not a script.

```text
  kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
          |
          v
   [ API server ] <----> [ etcd ]           control plane
     ^   ^    ^
     |   |    +---- scheduler: assigns unscheduled pods to nodes (by requests, affinity, taints)
     |   +--------- controller-manager: Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job ... controllers
     |
   watch / status
     |
   [ kubelet ] -> container runtime (containerd) -> your containers      each worker node
   [ kube-proxy or eBPF dataplane ] -> programs Service routing
```

## Pods, Deployments and ReplicaSets
A **pod** is the unit of scheduling: one or more containers that share a network namespace (same IP, talk over `localhost`) and can share volumes. Most pods run one app container, sometimes with sidecars (a log shipper, a service-mesh proxy) or init containers that run to completion first.

Pods are disposable. They get a new IP every time they are recreated, and you almost never create them directly. A **Deployment** declares a pod template and a replica count. It owns a **ReplicaSet** per template version, and each ReplicaSet keeps N pods alive.

A rolling update is the Deployment controller scaling a new ReplicaSet up while scaling the old one down, bounded by `maxSurge` (extra pods allowed above desired) and `maxUnavailable` (pods allowed below desired). Both default to 25%. `kubectl rollout undo` scales the previous ReplicaSet back up, which is why rollbacks are fast.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: api }
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: api }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:4b1e...
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: api-config }
          env:
            - name: DATABASE_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef: { name: api-secrets, key: database-url }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
            limits: { memory: 512Mi }
          startupProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
            failureThreshold: 30
            periodSeconds: 2
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec: { command: ["sleep", "5"] }
```

Other workload types: **StatefulSet** (stable names and per-pod volumes, for databases and brokers), **DaemonSet** (one pod per node: log agents, CNI), **Job** and **CronJob** (run to completion).

## Services: how a request reaches your container
A **Service** gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name (`api.default.svc.cluster.local`) to the set of pods matching its label selector. The control plane keeps **EndpointSlices** listing the IPs of matching pods that are **ready**. kube-proxy (iptables or IPVS rules) or an eBPF dataplane such as Cilium rewrites traffic for the virtual IP to one of those pod IPs.

Service types:
- **ClusterIP** (default): reachable only inside the cluster.
- **NodePort**: also opens a port on every node.
- **LoadBalancer**: asks the cloud provider for an external load balancer pointing at the nodes or pods.

For HTTP from the outside world you usually want one L7 entry point routing by host and path. **Ingress** is the original API for that, implemented by a controller you install. Ingress is feature-frozen; its successor is the **Gateway API** (`Gateway`, `HTTPRoute`), which separates the infrastructure owner's concerns (the gateway) from the app team's routes and supports traffic splitting by weight natively. The Kubernetes project also announced in late 2025 that the community ingress-nginx controller is being retired, which pushed many teams toward Gateway API implementations. For new clusters, start with Gateway API.

```text
client -> DNS -> cloud LB -> Gateway / Ingress controller pods
       -> HTTPRoute (host api.acme.com, path /v1) -> Service "api" (ClusterIP)
       -> EndpointSlice (ready pod IPs only) -> pod 10.2.3.17:8080 -> container
```

## Configuration and secrets
- **ConfigMaps** hold non-secret config, injected as env vars or mounted files. Mounted files update in place (eventually); env vars only change when the pod restarts. A common trick is to hash the config into a pod annotation so a config change triggers a rollout.
- **Secrets** are the same shape, but stored base64-encoded, which is encoding, not encryption. By default they sit unencrypted in etcd unless the cluster enables encryption at rest (managed clusters often do, with a cloud KMS). Lock them down with RBAC: anyone who can create a pod in the namespace can mount any secret in it.
- In practice, the source of truth lives in a real secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Vault) and is synced in by the External Secrets Operator or mounted with the Secrets Store CSI driver. Pods authenticate to the cloud with workload identity (IRSA or EKS Pod Identity on AWS, Workload Identity on GKE) instead of static keys.
- Never bake config or secrets into the image. The same image should run in staging and production with different config, as the twelve-factor app put it.

## Probes
| Probe | On failure | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| startup | Container restarted after `failureThreshold x periodSeconds`; other probes wait until it passes | Slow boots (JVM warm-up, migrations, cache load) |
| readiness | Pod removed from Service endpoints; **not** restarted | "Can I take traffic right now?" (warming up, overloaded, draining) |
| liveness | Container restarted | "Is this process wedged beyond recovery?" (deadlock) |

Rules that prevent outages:
- **Liveness checks only the process.** If liveness calls the database, a database blip restarts every replica simultaneously, and the restart storm (cold caches, connection floods) makes recovery slower.
- **Readiness can include critical dependencies**, but think about what happens if all pods go unready together: the Service has zero endpoints and every request fails anyway. Many teams keep readiness local too, and handle dependency failure inside the app with timeouts and fallbacks.
- **Use a startup probe instead of a huge `initialDelaySeconds`** on liveness.
- Make probe endpoints cheap and give them timeouts; a probe that takes 2 seconds under load will fail exactly when you are busiest.

## Requests, limits and QoS
- **Requests** are what the scheduler reserves. A pod only lands on a node with enough unreserved capacity. Requests also set the CPU share under contention.
- **Limits** are hard caps enforced by cgroups. CPU over the limit is **throttled** (CFS quota per 100 ms period), which shows up as latency spikes even when node CPU looks idle. Memory over the limit gets the container **OOM-killed** (`OOMKilled`, exit code 137).
- **QoS classes**: *Guaranteed* (requests equal limits for every container), *Burstable* (some requests set), *BestEffort* (nothing set). Under node memory pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort first, then Burstable pods using more than they requested.

A widely used, though debated, policy: set memory request equal to memory limit (memory is not compressible, so overcommitting it invites OOM kills), set CPU requests from observed usage, and leave CPU limits off for latency-sensitive services so they can burst into idle CPU. Whatever you choose, base numbers on measured p95 usage, not guesses. Runtimes need to know their limits too: recent Node.js versions and JVMs read cgroup limits, but check heap settings (`--max-old-space-size`, `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`).

## The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
The HPA periodically (every 15 seconds by default) reads a metric and computes:

```text
desiredReplicas = ceil( currentReplicas x currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue )

4 pods at 90% CPU, target 60%  ->  ceil(4 x 90 / 60) = 6 pods
```

- CPU utilisation is a percentage **of requests**, so a pod with tiny requests looks "busy" constantly and one with inflated requests never scales.
- A 10% tolerance avoids flapping; scale-down uses a stabilisation window (300 seconds by default) so a brief dip does not remove pods you will need again.
- `autoscaling/v2` supports memory, custom metrics (requests per second, in-flight requests) and external metrics (queue depth). KEDA builds on HPA for event sources like Kafka lag or SQS depth and can scale to zero.
- The HPA only adds pods. If no node has room, pods sit `Pending` until the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter adds nodes, which takes minutes. That lag is why you keep headroom.
- Do not let HPA and VPA fight over the same metric on the same workload.

## Graceful shutdown and disruptions
When a pod is deleted, two things happen in parallel: the kubelet sends SIGTERM, and the endpoints controller removes the pod from Services. Proxies on every node learn about the removal asynchronously, so for a moment traffic can still arrive at a process that has started shutting down. The `preStop` sleep above delays SIGTERM by a few seconds to cover that window. Your app must then drain in-flight requests before `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` expires.

A **PodDisruptionBudget** (`minAvailable: 2`) stops voluntary disruptions, such as node drains during upgrades, from taking down too many replicas at once. Spread replicas across zones with `topologySpreadConstraints` so one zone failure does not take all of them.

## When not to use Kubernetes
Kubernetes is an operating system for a fleet. If you have one or two services and a small team, a managed container platform (Cloud Run, ECS on Fargate, App Runner, Fly.io, Render) or a PaaS gets you rolling deploys, autoscaling and TLS without running a cluster, an ingress, cert-manager, a secrets operator and upgrades every few months. Reach for Kubernetes when you have many services, need its ecosystem (operators, GitOps, service mesh), or need portability across clouds.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- `kubectl describe pod` first: events show `ImagePullBackOff`, `FailedScheduling` (insufficient CPU or memory, taints), probe failures.
- `CrashLoopBackOff`: read `kubectl logs --previous`; check exit code (137 is OOM or SIGKILL, 1 is the app).
- `Pending` forever: requests bigger than any node, or no autoscaler capacity.
- Service has no endpoints: selector labels do not match pod labels, or pods are not ready.
- Latency spikes with idle nodes: CPU throttling; look at `container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total`.
- 502s during every deploy: no preStop delay or the app exits on SIGTERM without draining.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you understand reconciliation, how traffic actually flows, and the operational knobs that cause outages (probes, limits, shutdown). Seniors get asked about multi-zone resilience, autoscaling lag and when Kubernetes is overkill.

**A 60-second answer outline** for "how would you run this service on Kubernetes?":
1. Deployment with 3+ replicas spread across zones, image pinned by digest, PDB.
2. Requests from measured usage, memory limit, startup/readiness/liveness probes with liveness kept local.
3. ClusterIP Service behind a Gateway API route with TLS; config in ConfigMaps, secrets synced from a secret manager via workload identity.
4. HPA on CPU or a request-rate metric with min replicas for headroom, Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter for nodes.
5. Graceful shutdown with preStop and SIGTERM draining; rolling updates with `maxUnavailable: 0`.

**Follow-ups to expect:** What happens step by step when you run `kubectl apply`? Why did my pod get OOM-killed when the node had free memory? Why is my service slow even though CPU is at 30%? How does a Service pick a pod? Ingress versus Gateway API?
keyPoints: Kubernetes is a set of controllers that continuously reconcile actual state toward the desired state you store in the API server.
A Deployment manages ReplicaSets that manage pods; a Service gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name to whichever pods match its label selector.
Readiness controls traffic, liveness controls restarts, startup protects slow boots; a liveness probe that checks dependencies causes cascading restarts.
The scheduler places pods by requests; exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOM-killed, exceeding a CPU limit only throttles it.
HPA computes replicas as ceil(current x currentMetric / target); CPU utilisation is measured against requests, so wrong requests mean wrong scaling.
interview: Explain pods, Deployments and Services in Kubernetes and how a request reaches your container.
What is the difference between liveness, readiness and startup probes, and how do they go wrong?
How do resource requests and limits work in Kubernetes, and what happens when a pod exceeds them?
How does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler decide how many replicas to run?
How do you manage configuration and secrets for applications running on Kubernetes?

check.q: Your liveness probe calls the database. The database has a 30-second hiccup. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Nothing, liveness probes are informational
Pods are removed from the Service but keep running
Every pod fails liveness and gets restarted at once, turning a short blip into a full outage
The HPA scales the Deployment up
check.why: Liveness failure restarts the container. A shared dependency failing makes all replicas fail together. Dependency checks belong in readiness at most, and liveness should test only the process itself.

check.q: A container has `requests.cpu: 250m` and `limits.cpu: 500m`, and a traffic spike needs 1 full core. What happens?
options: The container is OOM-killed
The container is throttled by the CFS quota to about half a core and latency rises
The pod is evicted immediately
The scheduler moves the pod to a bigger node
check.why: CPU is compressible: going over the limit means throttling, not killing. Memory is incompressible: going over the memory limit gets the container OOM-killed.

check.q: An HPA targets 60% average CPU utilisation. There are 4 replicas averaging 90%. Ignoring tolerance and stabilisation, how many replicas does it want?
check.why: desired = ceil(4 x 90 / 60) = ceil(6) = 6.

lessons.summary: CI versus continuous delivery versus deployment, pipeline stages, caching, build-once artifacts, a real GitHub Actions workflow, pipeline security and trunk-based development.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
A CI/CD pipeline is the automated path from "I pushed a commit" to "it is running in production", with enough checks along the way that you trust it. The value is not the YAML. It is that **small changes ship often, safely, and the same way every time**, so a release is a non-event instead of a weekend.

Three terms that interviewers expect you to separate cleanly:

- **Continuous integration (CI):** everyone integrates into the shared mainline at least daily, and every integration is verified by an automated build and test run. Martin Fowler's canonical article is explicit that CI is a practice, not a tool: if your branches live for two weeks, running Jenkins on them is not CI.
- **Continuous delivery:** main is **always releasable**. Every green build produces an artifact that could go to production at the push of a button. A human still decides when.
- **Continuous deployment:** every change that passes the pipeline goes to production automatically, with no human gate. This needs strong tests, progressive rollout and automatic rollback.

## How a good pipeline is shaped
```text
push / PR
   |
   v
[ fast checks ] lint, typecheck, unit tests          ~1-3 min, run in parallel
   |
   v
[ build ] compile + docker build (cached) -> image tagged :<git-sha>, push to registry
   |      scan (CVE), SBOM, sign
   v
[ integration ] service + real Postgres/Redis in containers, contract tests, migrations dry-run
   |
   v  (main branch only)
[ deploy staging ] same image digest -> smoke tests / e2e
   |
   v  (auto, or approval for continuous delivery)
[ deploy prod ] canary 5% -> metrics check -> 100%  (auto-rollback on SLO breach)
```

Principles behind that shape:

1. **Fail fast and cheap.** Run linters and unit tests before expensive integration suites. Developers wait on the slowest required check, so keep the PR pipeline around 10 minutes; beyond that, people batch changes and context-switch.
2. **Build once, promote the artifact.** The image built from commit `a1b2c3d` is pushed once, identified by its digest, and that exact digest goes to staging and then production. Rebuilding per environment invites "but it passed in staging".
3. **Environments differ only in config.** Same image, different environment variables and secrets.
4. **Everything is in version control:** pipeline definition, Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, Terraform. A pipeline change gets reviewed like code.
5. **The pipeline is the only way to production.** If people can `kubectl apply` from laptops, the audit trail and the guarantees are gone.

## Caching: where most of the speed comes from
- **Dependency caches**: `actions/setup-node` with `cache: npm` caches the npm download cache keyed on the lockfile hash. Generic `actions/cache` works for anything with a stable key.
- **Docker layer cache**: CI runners start empty, so without a remote cache every build is cold. `docker/build-push-action` supports `cache-from`/`cache-to` with `type=gha` (GitHub's cache service) or `type=registry`.
- **Build tool caches**: Turborepo, Nx, Bazel and Gradle can skip tasks whose inputs did not change and share results across machines.
- **Test selection and sharding**: split slow suites across parallel jobs (Playwright and Jest/Vitest support sharding); in monorepos only run what the change affects.

Cache keys must include everything that changes the output (lockfile hash, OS, tool version). A cache that restores stale output is worse than no cache.

## A real GitHub Actions workflow
```yaml
name: ci-cd
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test }
        ports: ["5432:5432"]
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres" --health-interval 5s --health-retries 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint && npm run typecheck
      - run: npm test
        env: { DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:test@localhost:5432/postgres }

  build:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read, packages: write, id-token: write }
    outputs:
      digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - id: push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

  deploy-prod:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    permissions: { contents: read, id-token: write }
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/gha-deploy-prod
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh "ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}@${{ needs.build.outputs.digest }}"
```

Things worth pointing out:
- `concurrency` cancels superseded runs on the same branch, saving minutes and avoiding two deploys racing.
- Top-level `permissions: contents: read` makes the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` read-only; jobs ask for more only when needed.
- `environment: production` hooks into GitHub environment protection rules: required reviewers, wait timers, branch restrictions, and environment-scoped secrets.
- The deploy job uses **OIDC** (`id-token: write`) to assume a cloud role. No AWS keys are stored anywhere.
- It deploys by **digest**, not tag.
- In a real repo, pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA (with the version in a comment) and let Dependabot or Renovate update them.

## Environments, approvals and GitOps
Two deployment styles:

- **Push-based**: the pipeline runs `helm upgrade` or `kubectl apply` against the cluster. Simple, but CI needs cluster credentials.
- **Pull-based GitOps**: CI only updates the image digest in a config repo; an in-cluster agent (Argo CD, Flux) notices and reconciles the cluster to match Git. The cluster never exposes credentials to CI, drift is detected and reverted, and rollback is `git revert`. OpenGitOps describes the principles (declarative, versioned, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled).

Manual approvals feel safe but often are not: a reviewer clicking "approve" on a diff of an image tag is not testing anything. Prefer automated gates (canary metrics, smoke tests) and keep human approval for genuinely risky changes or compliance requirements.

## Securing the pipeline
CI systems hold the keys to production, which makes them a favourite target. The March 2025 compromise of the popular `tj-actions/changed-files` action, where tags were repointed to malicious code that dumped secrets into build logs, is the case study everyone cites.

- **No long-lived cloud credentials.** Use OIDC federation; restrict the role trust policy to your repo, branch and environment (`sub` claim).
- **Least-privilege tokens.** Default `GITHUB_TOKEN` to read-only; grant `packages: write` or `id-token: write` per job.
- **Pin actions to commit SHAs**; prefer official or verified publishers; review updates.
- **Untrusted input.** `pull_request_target` runs with secrets on code from forks; avoid checking out and running PR code in it. Never interpolate PR titles or branch names directly into `run:` scripts (script injection); pass them via environment variables.
- **Protect main.** Required reviews, required status checks, no force pushes, signed commits if you need them.
- **Supply chain.** Lockfiles with `npm ci`, dependency scanning, SBOMs, signed images with provenance attestations (SLSA levels), signature verification at deploy.
- **Secrets hygiene.** Environment-scoped secrets, masked in logs; rotate anything that may have leaked.

## Trunk-based development
In trunk-based development, developers merge small changes into main (the trunk) at least daily, from branches that live hours or a day or two. Unfinished work is merged but hidden behind **feature flags** or built behind an abstraction (**branch by abstraction**) so main stays releasable.

Why teams prefer it over long-lived feature branches:
- **Merge pain grows super-linearly with branch age.** Two branches diverging for three weeks produce conflicts nobody understands; ten small merges produce trivial ones.
- **Integration bugs show up within hours**, while the author still remembers the change.
- **Code review is better** on 200-line diffs than on 4,000-line ones.
- **It is a prerequisite for continuous delivery.** If features live on branches, main is never a complete picture of what you will ship.

DORA's research (the four keys: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service) has repeatedly found trunk-based practices associated with better delivery performance. The cost is discipline: strong automated tests, feature-flag hygiene, and comfort shipping incomplete code that is switched off.

GitFlow (develop, release and hotfix branches) still fits products with versioned releases and long support windows, such as mobile apps waiting on store review or on-prem software, but it is a poor fit for a web service deployed many times a day.

## Trade-offs and when not to
- Continuous deployment to production is wrong for regulated changes that need sign-off, or when your test and monitoring coverage cannot catch bad releases. Continuous delivery with a button is a fine stop.
- Self-hosted runners are faster and cheaper at scale, but a self-hosted runner on a public repo can be abused by fork PRs. Use ephemeral runners.
- A huge end-to-end suite as a required check makes the pipeline slow and flaky. Keep e2e small and focused on critical journeys; push most coverage down to unit and integration tests.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Flaky tests** erode trust until people re-run until green. Track flake rate, quarantine and fix; never auto-retry silently forever.
- **Tests that pass locally, fail in CI**: time zones, parallelism, ordering, missing services. Run CI's container locally (`act` or the same Docker image).
- **Deploy succeeded but nothing changed**: deploying a mutable tag that the cluster had cached. Deploy by digest.
- **Cache poisoning**: a PR from a fork writing to a cache main reads from. Scope caches by branch.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you can design a pipeline from scratch and justify each stage, whether you know build-once-promote and OIDC, and whether you understand that CI/CD is about small batches and feedback speed, not tools.

**A 60-second answer outline** for "design a pipeline for this service":
1. On every PR: lint, typecheck, unit tests in parallel with dependency caching; integration tests against real dependencies in containers. Target about 10 minutes.
2. On merge to main: build the image once with layer caching, tag by SHA, scan, sign, push.
3. Deploy that digest to staging automatically, run smoke tests.
4. Promote to production via canary with automated metric checks and auto-rollback; GitOps so the cluster pulls from Git.
5. OIDC for cloud access, least-privilege tokens, pinned actions, protected main. Track DORA metrics to see if it works.

**Follow-ups to expect:** How do you handle database migrations in this pipeline? How do you keep it fast as the repo grows? What do you do about flaky tests? Push versus pull deploys? How would someone attack this pipeline?
keyPoints: CI means integrating to main at least daily with an automated build and tests; continuous delivery keeps main always releasable; continuous deployment releases every green commit automatically.
Build the artifact once, tag it with the commit SHA, and promote the same digest through every environment.
Fast feedback is a feature: cache dependencies and Docker layers, parallelise, run the cheapest checks first, and keep the main pipeline under about 10 minutes.
Use OIDC federation instead of long-lived cloud keys, least-privilege job permissions, and third-party actions pinned to commit SHAs.
Trunk-based development with short-lived branches and feature flags reduces merge pain and is strongly associated with high delivery performance in DORA research.
interview: What is the difference between continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
Design a CI/CD pipeline for a containerised web service. What stages does it have and why?
What is trunk-based development and why do high-performing teams prefer it over long-lived feature branches?
How do you secure a CI/CD pipeline and its credentials?

check.q: Staging passed, but production runs an image rebuilt from the same commit and it fails. Which practice would have prevented this class of bug?
options: Running the tests twice
Building once and promoting the same image digest to every environment
Using a bigger CI runner
Tagging images as latest
check.why: Rebuilding can pull different base images or dependency versions. Promoting the exact digest that was tested means production runs the bytes you verified.

check.q: What is the main security advantage of OIDC federation from GitHub Actions to a cloud provider?
options: It makes builds faster
It encrypts the repository
Jobs get short-lived credentials scoped by repo, branch or environment, so no long-lived cloud key is stored in CI
It removes the need for IAM roles
check.why: The job exchanges a signed identity token for temporary credentials. The cloud role's trust policy can restrict which repository, branch or environment may assume it, and there is no static secret to leak.

check.q: Which is the best description of trunk-based development?
options: Everyone commits to main or merges short-lived branches into it at least daily, keeping main releasable and hiding unfinished work behind flags
Each feature lives on its own branch until it is fully finished, however long that takes
Releases are cut from a develop branch every quarter
Only the tech lead may merge to main
check.why: Trunk-based development minimises divergence: small changes merged often, with incomplete features hidden behind flags or branch by abstraction rather than kept on long-lived branches.

lessons.title: Infrastructure as code with Terraform
lessons.summary: How Terraform works: providers, state, plan and apply, remote locked state, modules and layout, drift, moved and import blocks, and how it compares with OpenTofu, Pulumi and CDK.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Infrastructure as code (IaC) means your servers, networks, databases, DNS records and IAM policies are described in files under version control, and a tool makes reality match those files. Martin Fowler's short definition still holds: define infrastructure through source code that can be treated like any software system, reviewed, tested and versioned.

What you get: reproducible environments (staging really looks like production), code review for infrastructure changes, an audit trail in Git, and disaster recovery that is "re-run the code" instead of "remember what we clicked in 2022".

Terraform is the most widely used tool for this. You write declarative HCL describing **resources**; **providers** (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Cloudflare, GitHub, Datadog, hundreds more) translate them into API calls. Terraform builds a dependency graph, works out what has to change, and calls the APIs in the right order, in parallel where it can.

## How Terraform works, step by step
```text
  *.tf config  --+
                 +--> terraform plan --> diff: create / update in place / replace / destroy
  state file   --+          ^
                            |
  real APIs  ---- refresh --+         terraform apply (that plan) --> API calls --> new state
```

1. **`terraform init`** downloads providers and modules and configures the backend where state lives. The dependency lock file `.terraform.lock.hcl` pins provider versions; commit it.
2. **`terraform plan`** reads the state, refreshes it against the real APIs, compares the result with your config, and prints the actions: `+` create, `~` update in place, `-/+` replace (destroy then create, or create before destroy if configured), `-` destroy.
3. **`terraform apply`** executes the plan. In automation you save the plan (`plan -out=tfplan`) and apply exactly that file, so what was reviewed is what runs.

A small example:

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.10"
  required_providers {
    aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 6.0" }
  }
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "acme-tf-state"
    key          = "prod/network/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.region
  default_tags { tags = { env = var.env, owner = "platform", managed_by = "terraform" } }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "uploads" {
  bucket = "acme-${var.env}-uploads"
  lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "uploads" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.uploads.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

output "uploads_bucket" { value = aws_s3_bucket.uploads.bucket }
```

The reference `aws_s3_bucket.uploads.id` creates an implicit dependency, so the access block is created after the bucket. `default_tags` stamps every resource with ownership tags, which pays off when you read the cloud bill.

## State: what it is and why it exists
The state file maps each **resource address** in your config (`aws_s3_bucket.uploads`) to a **real object** (bucket `acme-prod-uploads`) along with its last known attributes. Terraform needs it because:

- Most cloud resources cannot be reliably found from config alone (what is the ID of "the" load balancer?).
- It records dependencies so Terraform can destroy things in the right order even after they are deleted from config.
- It caches attributes so large plans do not hit every API for everything.

State is also dangerous:
- **It contains secrets in plain text**: database passwords, generated keys, anything a resource returns. Treat the state bucket like a secrets store: encrypted, versioned, tightly scoped IAM, never committed to Git.
- **Concurrent writes corrupt it.** Use a backend with **locking**. On AWS the S3 backend historically used a DynamoDB table for locks; since Terraform 1.10 it can lock with a lock file in S3 itself (`use_lockfile = true`), and the DynamoDB option is deprecated. Terraform Cloud/HCP Terraform, GCS and Azure Blob backends lock natively.
- **Losing it is painful.** Turn on bucket versioning so you can roll back a bad state write.

Never hand-edit state. Use `terraform state mv`, `state rm`, or better, the declarative blocks below, which go through code review.

## Modules and environment layout
A **module** is a directory of `.tf` files with input variables and outputs. Use them to encode a paved road ("a service gets an ECR repo, an IAM role, a log group with 30-day retention, and alarms") and version them (a private registry as below, or Git tags with `?ref=`) so changing a module does not silently change every consumer.

```hcl
module "orders_db" {
  source         = "app.terraform.io/acme/postgres/aws"
  version        = "3.2.0"
  name           = "orders"
  env            = var.env
  instance_class = var.env == "prod" ? "db.r7g.large" : "db.t4g.medium"
  multi_az       = var.env == "prod"
}
```

**Split state by blast radius.** One giant state for everything means every plan is slow, every apply can touch everything, and one mistake has an unlimited blast radius. A common layout:

```text
infra/
  modules/            network/, service/, postgres/  (versioned)
  live/
    prod/
      network/        own state
      data/           own state (databases change rarely; keep them away from churn)
      services/api/   own state
    staging/
      ...
```

Separate directories per environment (with separate state and often separate cloud accounts) are clearer than Terraform CLI workspaces for long-lived environments, because the differences are visible in code and credentials are naturally separated. Tools like Terragrunt or Terramate help keep these DRY.

**`for_each` over `count`.** With `count`, resources are indexed `[0]`, `[1]`, `[2]`; removing the first element shifts every index and Terraform plans to destroy and recreate the rest. `for_each` over a map or set keys resources by name, so removing one touches only that one.

## Refactoring and adoption without destroying things
Terraform tracks objects by address, so renaming a resource looks like "destroy the old one, create a new one" unless you tell it otherwise:

```hcl
moved {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.logs
  to   = module.logging.aws_s3_bucket.this
}

import {
  to = aws_route53_zone.main
  id = "Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ"
}

removed {
  from = aws_instance.legacy
  lifecycle { destroy = false }
}
```

- `moved` (Terraform 1.1+) records a rename or a move into a module.
- `import` blocks (1.5+) adopt existing resources through a reviewed plan; `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` can write a first draft of the config.
- `removed` (1.7+) stops managing a resource without destroying it.

## Drift
Drift is any difference between the real infrastructure and what the code and state say: someone changed a security group in the console during an incident, an autoscaler changed a desired count, another tool modified a tag.

**Detect it:** run `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` on a schedule (exit code 2 means changes are pending) or `terraform plan -refresh-only` to see what changed outside Terraform without proposing to change anything. HCP Terraform, Spacelift, env0 and similar platforms offer scheduled drift detection.

**Handle it:** for each drifted attribute decide: was the manual change right? Then **codify** it in the config and apply. Was it wrong? Then **revert** by applying the code. For attributes another system legitimately owns (an autoscaling group's desired capacity), tell Terraform to ignore them with `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [desired_capacity] }`.

**Prevent it:** remove console write access in production (read-only roles, break-glass access that is audited), and make the pipeline the only path to apply.

## Terraform in a pipeline
```text
PR opened  -> fmt -check, validate, tflint, policy checks (OPA/Conftest, Checkov)
           -> terraform plan per affected stack -> plan posted as PR comment
PR merged  -> apply the saved plan (OIDC role per environment) -> post result
nightly    -> plan -detailed-exitcode on every stack -> alert on drift
```

Tools like Atlantis or HCP Terraform run this flow. Policy as code catches "public S3 bucket" or "security group open to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22" before it exists.

## Alternatives and how to choose
| Tool | Language | State | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Terraform | HCL | Its own state file | Biggest provider ecosystem; licence changed to the Business Source License in 2023; HashiCorp is now part of IBM |
| OpenTofu | HCL | Same model | Open-source fork of Terraform under the Linux Foundation, created after the licence change; largely drop-in, adds features such as client-side state encryption |
| Pulumi | TypeScript, Python, Go, C#, Java | Pulumi Cloud or self-managed backend | Real loops, functions, types and unit tests; many providers bridged from Terraform's |
| AWS CDK | TypeScript, Python, Java, C#, Go | CloudFormation stacks (AWS holds state) | AWS only; high-level constructs; synthesises CloudFormation, so you inherit its rollback behaviour and limits |
| CloudFormation | YAML/JSON | AWS-managed | No state file to manage; AWS only |
| Crossplane | Kubernetes CRDs | The Kubernetes API | Continuous reconciliation, fits platform teams already all-in on Kubernetes |

How I would choose in an interview: multi-cloud or many SaaS providers and a team comfortable with declarative config points to Terraform or OpenTofu. A team of application developers who want to share types and logic with their app code leans to Pulumi or CDK. AWS-only shops with strong CloudFormation experience can use CDK happily. The worst choice is two tools managing the same resources.

## Trade-offs and common mistakes
- **Clever HCL** (nested dynamic blocks, maps of maps of objects) becomes unreadable. Boring and explicit wins.
- **Secrets in variables or outputs** end up in state and CI logs. Mark them `sensitive = true`, and better, let the cloud generate them (managed master passwords stored in a secret manager).
- **Unpinned providers** break builds when a major version lands. Pin with `~>` and commit the lock file.
- **Applying from laptops** with personal credentials: no audit trail, inconsistent versions, drift. Apply from CI.
- **Long-running applies that time out** midway leave partial state. Smaller stacks help; re-running plan shows what is left.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you understand state (what, why, risks), the plan review discipline, how to structure code for a team, and drift. Seniors get asked about blast radius, refactoring without downtime, and tool choice.

**A 60-second answer outline** for "how do you manage infrastructure with Terraform in a team?":
1. Remote state per environment and per stack, encrypted, versioned, locked, least-privilege access.
2. Versioned modules for the paved road; `for_each`, explicit tags, provider versions pinned.
3. PRs run fmt, validate, lint, policy checks and a plan posted for review; merges apply the saved plan from CI with OIDC.
4. Destroy and replace actions are red flags; critical resources use `prevent_destroy`; refactors use `moved` and `import` blocks.
5. Nightly drift detection, no console writes in production.

**Follow-ups to expect:** What is in the state file and why is it sensitive? What happens if two people apply at once? How do you rename a resource without recreating it? Workspaces versus directories? Why might you pick Pulumi?
keyPoints: Terraform compares your configuration with its state file and the real API to compute a plan; state is the mapping from resource addresses to real-world IDs.
Keep state remote, locked, encrypted and access-controlled; it often contains secrets in plain text.
Review the saved plan and apply exactly that plan; watch for destroy and replace actions, which are where outages come from.
Split state by environment and blast radius, compose reusable versioned modules, and prefer for_each over count for collections.
Drift is inevitable; detect it with scheduled plan or refresh-only runs, then either codify the change or revert it.
interview: What is Terraform state, why does it exist, and how do you manage it safely in a team?
How do you detect and handle infrastructure drift?
Terraform, Pulumi or AWS CDK: how would you choose an infrastructure-as-code tool?

check.q: A plan shows `-/+ resource "aws_db_instance" "main" (forces replacement)` after you renamed the database identifier. What should you do?
options: Apply it; Terraform will migrate the data
Run apply with -auto-approve to save time
Delete the state file and re-run
Stop: replacement destroys the database; revert the change or plan a migration, and consider prevent_destroy
check.why: Forces replacement means destroy and recreate. For a database that is data loss. Treat replace and destroy actions in a plan as a review red flag, and protect critical resources with lifecycle prevent_destroy.

check.q: Two engineers run `terraform apply` against the same state at the same moment. What prevents corruption?
options: State locking in the backend
Terraform's dependency graph
Provider retries
Workspaces
check.why: Backends that support locking let only one operation write the state at a time; the second run waits or fails. Without locking, concurrent applies can lose resources from state.

check.q: You refactor `aws_s3_bucket.logs` into a module, so its address becomes `module.logging.aws_s3_bucket.this`. How do you avoid Terraform destroying and recreating the bucket?
options: Add `count = 1` to the module
Add a `moved` block from the old address to the new one
Run terraform refresh
Rename the bucket in the console
check.why: Terraform tracks resources by address. A moved block tells it the existing object now lives at the new address, so the plan shows a move instead of destroy plus create.

lessons.title: Cloud primitives: compute, storage, networking, databases and IAM
lessons.summary: The building blocks every cloud shares: compute options, object, block and file storage, VPCs and security groups, managed databases, IAM least privilege, regions and zones.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Every major cloud sells the same handful of primitives under different names: somewhere to run code, somewhere to keep bytes, a private network to connect them, managed databases, and an identity system that decides who may do what. If you understand the primitives and their failure boundaries, you can design on AWS, Google Cloud or Azure and translate between them.

| Primitive | AWS | Google Cloud | Azure |
|---|---|---|---|
| VMs | EC2 | Compute Engine | Virtual Machines |
| Managed containers | ECS/Fargate, App Runner | Cloud Run | Container Apps |
| Kubernetes | EKS | GKE | AKS |
| Functions | Lambda | Cloud Run functions | Functions |
| Object storage | S3 | Cloud Storage | Blob Storage |
| Block storage | EBS | Persistent Disk | Managed Disks |
| Private network | VPC | VPC | Virtual Network |
| Relational DB | RDS, Aurora | Cloud SQL, AlloyDB | Azure SQL, Database for PostgreSQL |
| Key-value / document | DynamoDB | Firestore, Bigtable | Cosmos DB |
| Identity | IAM | IAM | Entra ID + RBAC |

This lesson uses AWS names because they are the most common in interviews; the ideas carry over.

## Compute: choosing how much to manage
```text
more control, more ops                                      less control, less ops
  VMs (EC2)  ->  Kubernetes (EKS)  ->  managed containers (Fargate, Cloud Run)  ->  functions (Lambda)
  you patch OS     you run workloads     you ship an image                         you ship a handler
```

- **VMs**: full control (kernel tuning, GPUs, special networking, licensed software). You own patching, scaling groups, images.
- **Kubernetes**: a platform for many services; powerful, but someone runs it.
- **Managed containers**: you provide an image, the platform runs and scales it. The sweet spot for many teams.
- **Functions**: event-driven, scale to zero, per-invocation billing, with limits on duration and runtime (see the serverless lesson).

Also choose architecture and family: ARM instances (AWS Graviton, Google Axion, Azure Cobalt) are typically cheaper per unit of performance for workloads that run on ARM, which most Node, Python, Go and Java services do.

## Storage: object, block, file
- **Object storage (S3, GCS, Blob)**: a flat namespace of keys to immutable objects over HTTP. Effectively unlimited, very durable (S3 is designed for eleven nines of durability), cheap, with storage classes for cold data. S3 has offered strong read-after-write consistency since December 2020. Use it for uploads, static assets, backups, logs, data lakes. Not a filesystem: no partial in-place updates, no rename, per-request pricing, latency in tens of milliseconds.
- **Block storage (EBS, Persistent Disk)**: a virtual disk attached to one VM (mostly), formatted with a filesystem. Low latency, provisioned IOPS and throughput. **Zonal**: an EBS volume lives in one AZ and cannot attach to an instance in another; snapshots go to regional storage. Use it for database data directories, boot disks.
- **File storage (EFS, Filestore, Azure Files)**: a managed NFS/SMB share many machines mount at once. Use it for legacy apps that need a shared POSIX filesystem. More expensive per GB and slower than block for heavy random I/O.

Rule of thumb for app engineers: put user files in object storage behind presigned URLs, keep servers stateless, and let the database own its disks.

## Networking: VPCs, subnets and the request path
A **VPC** is your private network in a region, with a CIDR range like `10.0.0.0/16`. You divide it into **subnets**, each in one availability zone.

- A **public subnet** has a route `0.0.0.0/0 -> internet gateway`. Resources with public IPs there are reachable from the internet (subject to security groups).
- A **private subnet** has no route to the internet gateway. Outbound internet access, if needed, goes through a **NAT gateway** that lives in a public subnet.
- **Security groups** are stateful firewalls attached to network interfaces; allow rules only; they can reference other security groups ("allow 5432 from the app's SG"), which is much better than IP ranges.
- **Network ACLs** are stateless, subnet-level, allow and deny rules. Most teams leave them permissive and rely on security groups.
- **VPC endpoints** (gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, interface endpoints via PrivateLink for other services) let private subnets reach cloud APIs without NAT, which is both safer and cheaper.

A standard three-tier layout:

```text
                         internet
                            |
                     [ internet gateway ]
   VPC 10.0.0.0/16          |
   +------------- AZ a -----------------+------------- AZ b ----------------+
   | public  10.0.0.0/24                | public  10.0.1.0/24               |
   |   ALB node, NAT gateway            |   ALB node, NAT gateway           |
   | private 10.0.10.0/24 (app)         | private 10.0.11.0/24 (app)        |
   |   ECS tasks / EKS nodes  SG: app   |   ECS tasks / EKS nodes  SG: app  |
   | private 10.0.20.0/24 (data)        | private 10.0.21.0/24 (data)       |
   |   RDS primary   SG: db (5432<-app) |   RDS standby (sync replica)      |
   +------------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
   S3 via gateway endpoint (no NAT)     secrets via interface endpoint
```

Key decisions: only the load balancer is public; apps and databases have no public IPs; the database security group accepts traffic only from the app security group; one NAT gateway per AZ so an AZ failure does not cut off egress for the others (cheaper setups share one and accept the risk).

Load balancers: an **ALB** works at L7 (HTTP routing by host and path, TLS termination, WebSockets); an **NLB** works at L4 (TCP/UDP, static IPs, very high throughput). In front of that, a CDN (CloudFront, Cloudflare) caches static content and absorbs attacks.

## Managed databases
Managed relational databases (RDS, Cloud SQL) handle provisioning, patching, backups with point-in-time recovery, and failover. What you still own: schema, indexes, queries, connection management, capacity and cost.

- **Multi-AZ** keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ; failover is automatic, typically within a minute or two, and your app must reconnect (DNS changes, so do not cache the IP forever). The standby does not serve reads in the classic setup.
- **Read replicas** are asynchronous copies for read scaling; they lag, so reads after writes may be stale.
- **Aurora** separates compute from a distributed storage layer replicated across three AZs, giving faster failover and replicas sharing storage.
- **DynamoDB** and similar are serverless key-value stores: single-digit millisecond reads at any scale if you model access patterns up front, painful if you need ad-hoc queries.
- **Connection limits** are the classic failure with serverless or heavily autoscaled apps: hundreds of pods each holding a pool of 10 connections can exhaust Postgres. Use a pooler (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer) and size pools deliberately.

## IAM and least privilege
IAM answers "can this principal perform this action on this resource under these conditions?"

- **Principals**: human users (ideally through SSO, not IAM users), roles assumed by services, federated identities from CI (OIDC) or Kubernetes (workload identity).
- **Policies**: JSON documents of `Effect`, `Action`, `Resource`, `Condition`. Evaluation: everything is implicitly denied, an explicit allow grants, and **an explicit deny always wins**. Organisation-level guardrails (Service Control Policies) and permission boundaries cap what any policy in an account can grant.
- **Roles and temporary credentials**: workloads assume roles and receive short-lived credentials from STS. Long-lived access keys are the thing that leaks on GitHub.

A least-privilege policy for a service that reads and writes one bucket prefix:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-prod-uploads/avatars/*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "kms:Decrypt",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:123456789012:key/1111aaaa-22bb-33cc-44dd-555555eeeeee",
      "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:ViaService": "s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com" } }
    }
  ]
}
```

How least privilege works in practice, because nobody writes perfect policies on day one:
1. **One role per workload**, never a shared "app" role.
2. **Start from what the code calls**, scope resources by ARN and prefix, avoid `*` actions.
3. **Use conditions**: source VPC endpoint, required tags, MFA for humans, `aws:PrincipalOrgID`.
4. **Review actual usage**: IAM Access Analyzer can generate policies from CloudTrail activity and flag unused permissions and external access.
5. **Separate accounts per environment** (AWS Organizations): the strongest IAM boundary is a different account. A bug in staging cannot touch production data.
6. **Break-glass access** for humans in production: time-limited, audited elevation instead of standing admin.

## Regions and availability zones
- A **region** is a geographic area (eu-west-1, us-central1) with independent infrastructure and control planes.
- An **availability zone** is one or more discrete data centres in a region with independent power, cooling and networking, close enough for low-latency synchronous replication (single-digit milliseconds between AZs).
- Some services are **zonal** (an EC2 instance, an EBS volume), some **regional** (S3, DynamoDB, an ALB spanning AZs), a few **global** (IAM, Route 53, CloudFront). The AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries whitepaper maps this out, including the point that global services' control planes often live in one region.

**Multi-AZ** is the default for production: spread replicas across at least two, usually three, AZs; use regional or multi-AZ managed services. It protects against the most common large failures at modest cost (mostly cross-AZ data transfer and extra standby capacity).

The AWS Builders' Library article on **static stability** adds the important nuance: do not rely on scaling up during a zone failure, because everyone else is scaling too and the control plane may be impaired. Pre-provision enough capacity that losing one AZ is absorbed by what is already running. With three AZs, that means running each at roughly two-thirds of the capacity needed to carry its share alone.

**Multi-region** protects against a whole region failing and lets you serve users closer to home, but it is a different class of problem: data replication across tens to hundreds of milliseconds, conflict resolution or a single write region, failover runbooks you must rehearse, and roughly double the cost. Common patterns: active-passive (warm standby in a second region, async replication, measured RTO and RPO) or active-active with a database built for it (DynamoDB global tables, Spanner, CockroachDB). Choose by the business's recovery time and recovery point objectives, not by fear.

## Trade-offs and common mistakes
- **Everything public** "for now": databases with public IPs and `0.0.0.0/0` security groups are how breaches start. Private by default.
- **Overlapping CIDRs** between VPCs make peering or Transit Gateway impossible later. Plan address space up front.
- **NAT gateway surprises**: every byte from private subnets to the internet or to S3 without an endpoint is charged per GB at the NAT. Add gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB on day one.
- **Single-AZ "production"** because the subnet group had one subnet.
- **Admin roles for everything**, and long-lived keys in CI. Use roles, OIDC and scoped policies.
- **Ignoring service quotas**: default limits (vCPUs per instance family, Lambda concurrency, IPs) block launches at the worst moment. Request increases ahead of launches.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** can you lay out a secure network, reason about failure domains, and treat IAM as a design concern rather than an afterthought? Seniors get asked about static stability, multi-region trade-offs and organisation-level guardrails.

**A 60-second answer outline** for "deploy this web app on AWS":
1. VPC across three AZs: public subnets for the ALB and NAT, private subnets for app tasks and the database, S3 and secret manager reached through VPC endpoints.
2. Containers on Fargate or EKS with one IAM role per service, scoped to exactly the bucket prefix and secrets it needs.
3. RDS Postgres Multi-AZ with automated backups and PITR, security group accepting only the app SG, connection pooling.
4. Static assets and uploads in S3 behind CloudFront; capacity sized to survive one AZ loss.
5. Separate accounts for prod and staging, SSO for humans, CloudTrail and budgets on.

**Follow-ups to expect:** What does a NAT gateway do and what does it cost? Security groups versus NACLs? What happens to your app during an RDS failover? Why might you go multi-region, and what breaks?
keyPoints: Pick compute by how much you want to manage: VMs, managed containers, Kubernetes or functions trade control for operational burden.
Object storage for blobs and static assets, block storage for a single machine's disk, file storage for shared POSIX access.
A typical VPC has public subnets for load balancers and NAT, private subnets for apps and data, spread across at least two availability zones.
IAM least privilege means short-lived role credentials, narrowly scoped actions and resources, conditions, and continuous review of what is actually used.
Availability zones protect against data-centre failure; regions protect against regional failure at a large cost in complexity and data consistency.
interview: Design a basic VPC for a web application with a database. What goes in public and private subnets?
How do you apply least privilege with cloud IAM in practice?
What are regions and availability zones, and how do you use them for high availability?
When would you use object, block and file storage?

check.q: Instances in a private subnet need to download packages from the internet but must not be reachable from it. What do they route through?
options: A NAT gateway in a public subnet
An internet gateway attached directly to the private subnet
A public IP on each instance
A network ACL that allows all traffic
check.why: A NAT gateway allows outbound connections initiated from the private subnet and blocks unsolicited inbound ones. Routing the private subnet to an internet gateway would make it public.

check.q: Which statement about AWS security groups and network ACLs is correct?
options: Both are stateless
Network ACLs attach to instances, security groups to subnets
Security groups only support deny rules
Security groups are stateful and attach to network interfaces; network ACLs are stateless and apply to subnets
check.why: Security groups track connections, so return traffic is allowed automatically, and they support allow rules only. NACLs evaluate each packet in both directions and support explicit deny.

check.q: Your service runs in three availability zones and must survive losing one zone without degrading. What is the highest safe steady-state utilisation per zone?
options: About 90%
About 33%
About 66%
100%, autoscaling will cover it
check.why: If one of three zones disappears, the remaining two must carry all the load, so each needs 50% more headroom: run at about two thirds. Autoscaling during a zonal event is unreliable because capacity is contested.
