lessons.title: Serverless functions and edge runtimes
lessons.summary: How function platforms run code, what cold starts cost and how to cut them, V8-isolate edge runtimes, the data-locality trap, cost maths, and when serverless fits.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
"Serverless" means you hand the platform a unit of code (a function, or a container) and it handles provisioning, scaling, patching and capacity, billing you for what you use instead of for machines. There are still servers; you just do not see, size or keep them.

Two families matter for interviews:

- **Regional functions and serverless containers**: AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Run, Azure Functions, Vercel Functions. Full language runtimes (Node.js, Python, Java, Go) running in a region, usually close to your database.
- **Edge runtimes**: Cloudflare Workers, Vercel's Edge runtime, Deno Deploy, Fastly Compute. Lightweight runtimes (mostly V8 isolates, or WebAssembly) deployed to hundreds of locations near users.

The trade-off throughout: you give up control and some predictability in exchange for not running infrastructure and paying nothing when idle.

## How a function platform runs your code
Using Lambda as the reference model, since its lifecycle is the best documented:

```text
request arrives
   |
   +-- warm environment free? --yes--> INVOKE handler (ms)
   |
   no
   v
COLD START
  1. place and boot a Firecracker microVM (sandbox)
  2. download and unpack your code or image
  3. start the runtime (Node.js, JVM, Python)
  4. INIT: run your module-scope code (imports, SDK clients, config fetch)
  5. INVOKE handler
   |
   v
environment stays warm for reuse ... eventually frozen, then reclaimed
```

Key facts:
- Each Lambda execution environment processes **one request at a time**. 100 concurrent requests need 100 environments; a burst beyond the warm pool means cold starts. (Cloud Run and Vercel's Fluid compute instead let one instance serve many concurrent requests, which reduces cold starts and idle cost for I/O-bound work.)
- Between invocations the environment is **frozen**. Background work you started after returning the response may not run until the next invocation, or ever. Flush logs and metrics before returning, or use the platform's "wait until" helper where it exists.
- Module-scope state survives across warm invocations of the same environment, which is great for caches and connection reuse, and a bug if you store per-request data there.
- Limits shape design: Lambda allows up to 15 minutes per invocation and 128 MB to 10,240 MB of memory, with CPU allocated in proportion to memory. Regional account concurrency has a default quota (1,000) that you can raise.

Marc Brooker and colleagues' Firecracker paper (NSDI 2020) explains why AWS built a microVM: VM-level isolation between tenants with boot times and memory overhead low enough for per-function sandboxes.

## Cold starts: what costs time and how to cut it
Cold-start time is sandbox creation plus runtime start plus **your init code**. The last part is usually the biggest one you control.

| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| Large bundle or image | Bundle and tree-shake (esbuild), drop unused SDKs, import only the AWS SDK v3 clients you use |
| Heavy init (ORM metadata, big config fetch) | Lazy-load rarely used modules; cache config; precompute at build time |
| Slow runtime start (JVM, .NET) | SnapStart (snapshot of the initialised environment), GraalVM native images, or a faster runtime |
| Bursty traffic beyond the warm pool | Provisioned concurrency (Lambda) or minimum instances (Cloud Run) |
| VPC attachment (historically) | Much improved since Lambda moved to shared network interfaces in 2019; not the multi-second penalty it once was |
| Low memory setting | More memory means more CPU, which often shortens init and duration enough to cost the same or less |

Order of magnitude: lean Node.js or Python functions often cold start in a few hundred milliseconds; a JVM function without SnapStart can take seconds. Measure your own: Lambda reports `Init Duration` in the REPORT log line for cold invocations.

```ts
import { DynamoDBClient } from "@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb";
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, GetCommand } from "@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb";

const db = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(new DynamoDBClient({}));

export const handler = async (event: { pathParameters?: { id?: string } }) => {
  const id = event.pathParameters?.id;
  if (!id) return { statusCode: 400, body: "missing id" };
  const { Item } = await db.send(new GetCommand({ TableName: process.env.TABLE, Key: { id } }));
  return Item ? { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify(Item) } : { statusCode: 404, body: "not found" };
};
```

The client lives in module scope, so it is created once per environment and its TCP/TLS connections are reused on warm invocations.

Provisioned concurrency and minimum instances remove cold starts for the configured capacity, but you pay for that capacity whether or not it is used. You are buying back a little bit of "server".

## Edge runtimes
Cloudflare's "How Workers works" page lays out the model: instead of a container or microVM per tenant, many customers' code runs as **V8 isolates** inside one process. An isolate has its own heap and globals but shares the runtime, so creating one takes milliseconds and costs little memory. That is what makes it economical to run your code in hundreds of locations and start it on demand.

What you trade:
- **A restricted API surface**: Web-standard APIs (`fetch`, `Request`, `Response`, Web Crypto, streams). Node.js compatibility layers have grown a lot, but native modules, raw TCP in some cases and filesystem access are limited or absent.
- **Tight CPU and memory limits** per request. Edge is for fast logic, not heavy computation.
- **Different databases**: drivers must speak HTTP or WebSockets (or use platform-provided connectors and poolers).

Good uses: redirects and rewrites, auth token checks, A/B bucketing, geolocation-based routing, header manipulation, personalising cached pages, serving from an edge key-value store, rate limiting near the source.

Note that Next.js 16 renamed `middleware.ts` to `proxy.ts` and runs it on the Node.js runtime by default, a sign that frameworks have moved away from pushing general logic into edge runtimes.

## The data-locality trap
Latency is dominated by **round trips to data**, not by where the code runs.

```text
user in Sydney, database in us-east-1 (Virginia), ~200 ms RTT between them

regional function in us-east-1:
  user -> function: 1 round trip  ~200 ms
  function -> DB x4 queries         ~1-2 ms each
  total                             ~210 ms

edge function in Sydney:
  user -> function: 1 round trip  ~10 ms
  function -> DB x4 sequential     ~200 ms each = 800 ms
  total                             ~810 ms
```

Edge wins only when the work needs no data, cached data, or data that is also replicated near the user (edge KV, read replicas in many regions, globally distributed databases). Vercel and Cloudflare both let you pin functions to a region near your database for exactly this reason. In an interview, saying "edge is faster" without this caveat is a red flag.

## Cost: the crossover
Function pricing is per request plus per GB-second of duration. Using Lambda's published x86 on-demand prices (about $0.20 per million requests and about $0.0000166667 per GB-second, before free tier; check current prices):

```text
steady 100 req/s, 100 ms average, 512 MB
requests per 30 days  = 100 x 2,592,000          = 259.2 M   -> ~$52
GB-seconds            = 259.2 M x 0.1 s x 0.5 GB = 12.96 M  -> ~$216
total                                                         ~$268 / month
```

Compare that with the price of the always-on containers or instances that could serve 100 req/s at your latency target, including headroom. For spiky or low traffic, functions win easily because idle costs nothing. For steady high throughput, always-on capacity (especially with savings plans) is usually cheaper, and the gap grows with load. Remember the hidden costs on both sides: API gateway charges, NAT and data transfer, logging volume, and on the container side, the engineers who run it.

## When serverless fits
- **Spiky or unpredictable traffic**, and things that are idle most of the time: internal tools, webhooks, cron jobs, prototypes.
- **Event-driven glue**: object uploaded, queue message arrived, record changed.
- **Embarrassingly parallel fan-out**: process 10,000 files with 1,000 concurrent invocations.
- **Small teams** who would rather not run infrastructure at all.

## When it does not
- **Steady, high, predictable load** where per-request pricing exceeds reserved capacity.
- **Long-running work** beyond duration limits: video transcoding, large ML jobs, long ETL. Use containers or batch services.
- **Long-lived connections**: WebSockets, gRPC streams, SSE beyond short windows. Platforms offer workarounds (API Gateway WebSockets, Durable Objects), each with its own model.
- **Heavy connection-pool databases**: thousands of concurrent environments each opening Postgres connections. Needs a pooler (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer, Prisma Accelerate, Neon or Supabase poolers) or an HTTP-based database.
- **Strict tail latency SLOs** where an occasional cold start breaks the budget, unless you pay for provisioned capacity.
- **GPU or specialised hardware**, large local disk, or kernel-level tuning.
- **Portability concerns**: deep coupling to one provider's event sources and IAM. Serverless containers (Cloud Run, Fargate) reduce lock-in compared with function-specific APIs.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- **Recursive triggers**: a function writes to the bucket that triggers it, and the loop runs up a bill. Use separate prefixes or buckets; Lambda now detects some recursive loops, but do not rely on it.
- **Unbounded concurrency** overwhelming a downstream database. Set reserved concurrency as a cap.
- **Retries without idempotency**: async invocations and queue triggers retry on failure, so handlers must tolerate duplicates.
- **Fire-and-forget work after the response**: it may never run once the environment is frozen.
- **Timeouts longer than the caller's**: an API gateway that times out at 30 seconds while the function keeps running and billing.
- **Debugging blind**: emit structured logs with request IDs, use tracing (X-Ray, OpenTelemetry), and watch `Init Duration`, throttles, errors and concurrency.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you know the execution model (environments, init versus invoke, concurrency), what really drives cold starts, the edge data-locality trap, and whether you can argue cost and fit with numbers rather than fashion.

**A 60-second answer outline** for "should we build this on serverless?":
1. Describe the traffic shape and latency SLO. Spiky or low traffic and relaxed tails point to functions; steady high throughput points to containers.
2. Check constraints: duration, connections (WebSockets, database pools), hardware, runtime.
3. Name cold-start mitigations: lean bundles, init outside the handler, provisioned concurrency or min instances for latency-critical paths.
4. Put compute next to the data; use edge only for data-free or cached logic.
5. Sketch the cost crossover with real numbers and include gateway, data transfer and logging.

**Follow-ups to expect:** What exactly happens during a cold start? How does Lambda concurrency differ from Cloud Run concurrency? How do you connect thousands of functions to Postgres? Why is my edge function slower than my old server?
keyPoints: A function platform keeps execution environments warm between requests; a cold start is creating one: microVM or isolate, runtime boot, and your init code.
Reduce cold starts with smaller bundles, lazy init, faster runtimes, provisioned concurrency or minimum instances, and snapshot-based starts like Lambda SnapStart.
Edge runtimes use V8 isolates that start in milliseconds near the user, with a restricted API and tight CPU limits.
Edge only helps when the data is also near the user; an edge function that makes several round trips to a distant database is slower than a regional one.
Serverless fits spiky, event-driven and low-to-moderate traffic; steady high throughput, long-lived connections, heavy compute and strict tail latency often fit containers better.
interview: What causes serverless cold starts and how do you reduce them?
When is serverless the wrong choice?
What is an edge runtime and when does running code at the edge actually make things faster?

check.q: In AWS Lambda, where should you create a database client so it is reused across invocations?
options: Inside the handler, so each request gets a fresh client
In a separate Lambda that the handler calls
In module scope outside the handler, so it is created once per execution environment
In an environment variable
check.why: Code outside the handler runs during the init phase, once per execution environment, and its objects survive across warm invocations. Creating clients per request adds latency and exhausts connections.

check.q: An edge function in Sydney makes four sequential queries to a Postgres primary in Virginia. What is the most likely result?
options: Faster than a regional function because the code runs close to the user
Slower than running the function next to the database, because each query pays a long intercontinental round trip
Identical latency
The edge runtime caches the queries automatically
check.why: Compute moved closer to the user but every database round trip now crosses the Pacific. Put compute near the data, or bring the data to the edge with caches or replicas.

check.q: Which workload is the weakest fit for classic per-request functions such as Lambda?
options: A webhook receiver that gets 50 requests a day
Resizing images when files land in a bucket
A nightly report job that takes 2 minutes
A service handling a steady 3,000 requests per second around the clock with long-lived WebSocket connections
check.why: Steady high throughput is usually cheaper on always-on containers, and long-lived connections do not match a per-invocation model with duration limits. The other three are classic serverless fits.

lessons.title: Deployment strategies, feature flags and safe migrations
lessons.summary: Rolling, blue-green and canary deploys, automated canary analysis, feature flags that separate deploy from release, fast rollbacks, and expand-and-contract migrations.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Most outages are caused by changes: a new binary, a config push, a schema migration. A deployment strategy is how you **limit the blast radius of a bad change and shorten the time it is live**. The goal is not zero bad deploys; it is that a bad deploy hurts few users for a few minutes and is undone automatically.

Two cautionary tales interviewers like:
- **Knight Capital (2012)**: a deploy reached seven of eight servers, and a repurposed flag activated dead code on the eighth. The firm lost about $440 million in 45 minutes. Lessons: deploy consistently, never reuse flags, have a fast kill switch.
- **CrowdStrike (July 2024)**: a faulty content update was pushed to all customers at once and crashed roughly 8.5 million Windows machines. Lesson: even "just config" needs staged rollout.

Marc Brooker's essay on software deployment, speed and safety makes the balancing point: going slower is not automatically safer, because slow, batched deploys carry more change per release. What makes deploys safe is small changes, staged exposure, good health signals and automatic rollback.

## The three strategies
```text
ROLLING        v1 v1 v1 v1  ->  v2 v1 v1 v1  ->  v2 v2 v1 v1  ->  v2 v2 v2 v2
               replace a few at a time; both versions serve traffic mid-rollout

BLUE-GREEN     [ blue v1  ] <- 100% traffic      [ blue v1  ]  (idle, kept for rollback)
               [ green v2 ]   (tested, idle)     [ green v2 ] <- 100% traffic
               switch the router in one step

CANARY         v1 95%  /  v2 5%   -> analyse -> 25% -> analyse -> 50% -> 100%
               widen exposure only while the canary is as healthy as the baseline
```

| | Rolling | Blue-green | Canary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Extra capacity | A little (`maxSurge`) | A full second environment during cutover | A little |
| Rollback speed | Minutes (roll back through instances) | Seconds (switch router back) | Seconds (shift weight to 0%) |
| Users exposed to a bad build | Grows with rollout progress | Everyone, at switch time | A small, controlled percentage |
| Needs | Readiness probes, compatibility | Router or DNS switch, warm-up, shared-state compatibility | Traffic splitting, good metrics, automated analysis |
| Default in | Kubernetes Deployments, ECS | ECS/CodeDeploy, many PaaS | Argo Rollouts, Flagger, service meshes, Spinnaker |

**Rolling** is the default because it is free: Kubernetes does it with `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`. Its weakness is that you find problems only after a meaningful fraction of the fleet runs the new version, and rollback is another rolling update.

**Blue-green** keeps two production environments. You deploy to the idle one, test it with real infrastructure, then flip the load balancer. Martin Fowler's article notes the elegant property that rollback is just flipping back. The catches: you pay for double capacity during the switch, a switch exposes everyone at once, caches and connection pools on green start cold, and both colours share the database, so schema changes still need care. DNS-based switching is slow and leaky because clients cache records; switch at the load balancer.

**Canary** routes a small slice (by percentage, region, internal users first, or a cell) to the new version and expands in steps. The Google SRE Workbook chapter on canarying is the reference: compare the canary against a **concurrent baseline** running the old version with similar traffic, not against yesterday's numbers, because traffic mix changes by the hour.

## Automated canary analysis
Humans watching dashboards miss things and get tired. Automate the gate:

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 5
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - analysis: { templates: [{ templateName: error-rate }] }
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - analysis: { templates: [{ templateName: error-rate }] }
        - setWeight: 100
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: error-rate
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: http-5xx-ratio
      interval: 1m
      failureLimit: 2
      successCondition: result[0] < 0.01
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="api",version="canary",code=~"5.."}[5m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{app="api",version="canary"}[5m]))
```

What to measure: error rate, latency percentiles (p99, not just average), saturation (CPU, memory, queue depth), and **business metrics** (checkouts per minute, login success). Crashes are easy to catch; a subtle 3% drop in conversions is not, unless you watch it.

Practical details:
- **Enough traffic** for statistical signal. A 1% canary on a service with 10 requests a minute tells you nothing; use longer bake times or bigger slices.
- **Bake time** catches slow problems: memory leaks, cache expiry effects, daily batch interactions.
- **Waves across failure domains**: the AWS Builders' Library article on hands-off deployments describes deploying to one box, then one AZ, then one region, then many regions in waves, with automatic rollback at every stage. Netflix's Kayenta and Spinnaker made automated canary analysis widely known.

## Feature flags: separate deploy from release
A **deploy** puts code on servers. A **release** exposes behaviour to users. Feature flags let you deploy dark code continuously and release it independently: to employees, then 1% of users, then a region, then everyone, and turn it off in seconds without a deploy.

Pete Hodgson's article on Martin Fowler's site classifies toggles, which helps in interviews:
- **Release toggles**: hide incomplete features; short-lived (days to weeks).
- **Experiment toggles**: A/B tests; live for the experiment.
- **Ops toggles**: kill switches and load-shedding switches; some are long-lived on purpose.
- **Permission toggles**: entitlements, beta programmes; often permanent and really product configuration.

```ts
const enabled = await flags.isEnabled("new-checkout", {
  userId: user.id,
  country: user.country,
  plan: user.plan,
});
return enabled ? renderNewCheckout(cart) : renderCheckout(cart);
```

Implementation notes: evaluate flags locally from a cached ruleset (SDKs of LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, GrowthBook, or OpenFeature as a vendor-neutral API) so a flag service outage does not take you down; define a safe default for when the ruleset is unavailable; use consistent hashing on user ID so a user stays in the same bucket.

Costs are real:
- **Combinatorial complexity**: 10 flags means 1,024 possible code paths. You cannot test them all; keep flags few and short-lived.
- **Flag debt**: dead flags and both code paths left in place forever. Give every flag an owner and expiry date, and remove the losing path once the flag is fully on.
- **Hidden config changes**: flipping a flag is a production change. Audit log it, and roll it out gradually like code.
- **Never repurpose a flag.** Knight Capital is the cautionary tale.

## Rollbacks and roll-forwards
Rollback means returning to the last known good **artifact**: re-point the Deployment at the previous image digest, shift canary weight to zero, flip blue-green back, or `git revert` in GitOps. It should be one command or one click, rehearsed, and faster than diagnosing.

Rules of thumb:
- **Mitigate first, debug second.** If a deploy correlates with an error spike, roll back now and investigate on the old version.
- **Rollback must be safe.** It is safe only if the previous version still works with the current data and schema, which is why migrations are designed backward compatible.
- **Roll forward** when rollback is impossible or riskier (a data format already written that the old version cannot read) and the fix is small and well understood.
- **Config and flags count.** A config push or flag flip is a deploy; keep the previous value one click away.

## Database migrations with deploys
During any rollout, **old and new code run at the same time** against the same database, and a rollback brings old code back. So every schema state must work with at least two adjacent code versions. The pattern is **expand and contract** (Danilo Sato's "ParallelChange" on Martin Fowler's site):

```text
goal: rename users.fullname -> users.display_name

deploy 1  EXPAND     add column display_name (nullable)          schema: both columns
deploy 2  DUAL WRITE code writes both, reads fullname             old + new code both fine
          BACKFILL   batch-copy fullname -> display_name for old rows (throttled)
deploy 3  SWITCH     code reads display_name, still writes both
deploy 4  STOP OLD   code stops writing fullname
deploy 5  CONTRACT   drop column fullname (after a safe delay)
```

Each step is independently deployable and reversible until the final drop. Tedious? Yes. It is also how teams change schemas on busy tables without downtime.

Operational rules for Postgres (similar ideas apply to MySQL with tools like gh-ost):
- Set `lock_timeout` (for example `SET lock_timeout = '5s'`) on migration sessions. `ALTER TABLE` needs a strong lock; if it queues behind a long query, every other query queues behind it and you have an outage.
- Build indexes with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (outside a transaction).
- Add `NOT NULL` constraints safely: add a `CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID` constraint, `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` later, then set `NOT NULL`.
- Adding a column with a constant default has been fast since Postgres 11; a volatile default still rewrites the table.
- Backfill in small batches with sleeps, not one giant `UPDATE` that bloats the table and lags replicas.
- Run migrations as a separate pipeline step (or a Kubernetes Job) before the code deploy that depends on them, never in every pod's startup where ten replicas race.

## Trade-offs and when not to bother
- A small internal app with a handful of users can use plain rolling deploys and a quick rollback; canary analysis needs traffic and metrics to be meaningful.
- Blue-green is attractive for stateful or slow-to-warm systems where mixed versions are awkward, if you can afford the capacity.
- Feature flags for every change are overkill; use them for risky or user-visible changes and incomplete work on trunk.

## Common mistakes and debugging
- Canary metrics that do not distinguish versions: label every metric with `version` or the pod template hash.
- Session or cache incompatibility between versions (a new serialised format the old version cannot read) breaks rollbacks; version your formats.
- Deploying migrations and code in one step, so rollback leaves code that does not match the schema.
- Long-running jobs or consumers killed mid-work by a deploy; drain them and make them resumable.
- "We will clean up the flag later". Put the removal ticket in the same sprint.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** that you know the strategies and their costs, that you think in blast radius and automated rollback, and above all that you understand the version-overlap problem for data and schemas. Senior candidates are expected to bring up expand and contract without being prompted.

**A 60-second answer outline** for "how would you deploy changes safely here?":
1. Small changes, built once and deployed by digest; risky behaviour behind flags.
2. Canary to 5%, automated comparison with a baseline on errors, p99 latency, saturation and a business metric; widen in steps with bake time; auto-rollback.
3. Rollback is one action and rehearsed; mitigate before debugging.
4. Schema changes via expand and contract, migrations run separately with lock timeouts, every step compatible with N-1.
5. Flags have owners and expiry dates; config pushes are staged like code.

**Follow-ups to expect:** How do you canary a service with little traffic? How do you roll back after a migration? Blue-green with a shared database: what breaks? How do you test feature-flag combinations? How do you deploy a breaking API change to mobile clients you cannot force-upgrade?
keyPoints: Rolling replaces instances gradually; blue-green switches all traffic between two full environments; canary sends a small slice to the new version and widens it while metrics stay healthy.
Automate the decision: compare canary and baseline on error rate, latency and saturation, and roll back without waiting for a human.
Feature flags decouple deploying code from releasing behaviour; they need owners, expiry dates and cleanup or they become debt.
Every deploy must be compatible with the previous version running at the same time: two versions always overlap during a rollout.
Change schemas with expand and contract: add, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, then remove, each step deployed and reversible on its own.
interview: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments.
How do you deploy a database schema change without downtime?
How do feature flags change the way you release software, and what are their costs?
A deploy just raised the error rate. Walk me through what you do.

check.q: You need to rename the column `users.fullname` to `display_name` with zero downtime. What is the safe first deploy?
options: ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN in the same deploy as the code change
Add `display_name`, have the code write both columns, and keep reading `fullname`
Drop `fullname` and add `display_name`
Take a maintenance window
check.why: Expand first: the new column exists and is kept in sync while old code still works. Backfill, switch reads, stop writing the old column, and only then drop it, each as its own deploy.

check.q: What is the main extra cost of blue-green compared with rolling deployments?
options: It cannot be automated
It is impossible to roll back
It requires feature flags
You need capacity for two full environments during the switch, and shared state such as the database still has to be compatible with both
check.why: Blue-green gives an instant switch and rollback but doubles capacity during the cutover, and both colours usually share one database, so schema changes still need backward compatibility.

check.q: A canary at 5% shows error rate 0.4% versus 0.1% on the baseline over 15 minutes. What should an automated analysis do?
options: Fail the canary and roll back automatically
Promote to 100%; 0.4% is a low error rate
Wait for a human to look at dashboards tomorrow
Increase to 50% to get more data
check.why: The canary is four times worse than the baseline under the same conditions. Comparing against a concurrent baseline, not an absolute threshold, is what canary analysis is for.

lessons.title: Autoscaling, capacity planning and cloud cost
lessons.summary: Scaling on the right signal, autoscaling lag and headroom, capacity planning with load tests and Little's law, FinOps and unit economics, pricing models and cost traps.
lessons.body:
## The core idea
Scaling and cost are the same problem viewed from two sides. Too little capacity and latency explodes and requests fail; too much and you pay for idle machines. Autoscaling tries to track demand automatically, capacity planning decides the floor, ceiling and headroom, and FinOps makes sure someone actually looks at the bill and connects it to the code that caused it.

The mindset interviewers want: **measure first** (what saturates, at what load, at what cost per unit of work), then design scaling and spending around those numbers.

## Scaling on the right signal
An autoscaler is a feedback loop: observe a metric, compare with a target, change capacity. It is only as good as the metric's relationship to saturation.

| Workload | Good signal | Why |
|---|---|---|
| CPU-bound API (JSON rendering, image work, crypto) | CPU utilisation (vs requests) | CPU tracks work done |
| I/O-bound API (waiting on DB and other services) | In-flight requests per pod, requests per second per pod, latency | CPU stays low while queues grow |
| Queue consumers | Queue depth or lag divided by per-worker throughput | Backlog is the demand |
| Streaming / Kafka consumers | Consumer lag per partition (capped at partition count) | More consumers than partitions do nothing |
| Memory-heavy caches | Usually do not autoscale horizontally; size them deliberately | Scaling a cache reshuffles keys |

Kubernetes gives you the HPA for pods (CPU, memory, custom and external metrics), KEDA for event sources such as SQS, Kafka, Redis or cron schedules (including scale to zero), and the VPA for right-sizing requests. Managed platforms scale on concurrency directly (Cloud Run's per-instance concurrency, Lambda's one request per environment).

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api }
  minReplicas: 6
  maxReplicas: 60
  metrics:
    - type: Pods
      pods:
        metric: { name: http_requests_in_flight }
        target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "40" }
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 30 }]
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 20, periodSeconds: 60 }]
```

This scales up aggressively (can double every 30 seconds) and down cautiously (20% per minute after five calm minutes), which is the right asymmetry: under-provisioning hurts users, over-provisioning for a few minutes costs pennies. Custom metrics like `http_requests_in_flight` need a metrics adapter (Prometheus Adapter, or KEDA).

## Autoscaling lag and headroom
```text
traffic spike at t=0
  metrics scraped and aggregated ........ 15-60 s
  HPA decides, pods created ............. seconds
  pods Pending: no room on nodes
  node autoscaler launches instances .... 1-3+ min (boot, join, pull image)
  app starts, warms caches, passes readiness ... seconds to minutes
capacity actually serving: often 2-5 minutes after the spike began
```

Implications:
- **Keep headroom**: target 50-70% utilisation, not 90%, so the current fleet absorbs the first minutes of a spike.
- **Make startup fast**: small images, lazy init, readiness that turns green quickly.
- **Speed up nodes**: Karpenter provisions right-sized nodes directly from pending pods, usually faster than node-group based scaling; some teams run low-priority "placeholder" pods that get preempted to free warm capacity instantly.
- **Pre-scale for known events**: scheduled scaling before a launch, a sale, or the daily 9 a.m. peak. Predictive scaling (EC2 Auto Scaling offers it) learns daily and weekly cycles.
- **Protect yourself when scaling cannot keep up**: rate limiting, load shedding of low-priority work, and graceful degradation. The Google SRE book chapter on handling overload covers per-client quotas and criticality-based shedding.
- **Downstreams have limits**: scaling the API from 10 to 100 pods can multiply database connections tenfold. Autoscaling must respect the tightest bottleneck.

## Capacity planning
Autoscaling handles minutes-to-hours variation. Capacity planning answers: what floor and ceiling, how much headroom, which quotas and reservations, for the next quarter.

1. **Find per-instance capacity at your SLO.** Load test one pod (k6, Gatling, Locust) with realistic traffic and increase load until p99 latency breaks the SLO or errors appear. That knee, minus a safety margin, is the per-pod throughput you plan with. Throughput at 100% CPU is not the number; latency degrades sharply well before that as queues build.
2. **Use Little's law** to reason about concurrency: `L = lambda x W`. At 2,000 req/s and 50 ms average latency there are 100 requests in flight; if each holds a DB connection for its full duration, the pool across all pods needs about 100 connections plus headroom.
3. **Forecast peak demand** from history: daily and weekly peaks, growth trend, planned launches, seasonality.
4. **Add failure headroom.** N+1 at minimum; to survive losing one of three AZs, each zone needs to carry half the load, so run at about two-thirds of zonal capacity.
5. **Check every dependency and quota**: database CPU and connections, cache memory, third-party rate limits, cloud quotas (vCPUs per family, IPs per subnet, Lambda concurrency).

```text
peak 6,000 req/s, per-pod capacity at SLO 250 req/s, keep 30% headroom
pods needed = 6,000 / (250 x 0.7) = 34.3 -> 35
spread over 3 AZs and survive one loss: each AZ must carry 50% of peak
  -> 6,000 x 0.5 / (250 x 0.7) = 17.1 -> 18 per AZ -> 54 pods at peak
minReplicas covers the normal daily trough plus one AZ loss; maxReplicas >= 54 with quota to match
```

## FinOps basics
The FinOps Foundation describes FinOps as an operating model where engineering, finance and business share accountability for cloud spend, working in a loop of **Inform** (visibility and allocation), **Optimize** (rates and usage), **Operate** (continuous governance).

What it means for an engineer:
- **Allocation**: tag every resource with team, service and environment (enforced in Terraform `default_tags` and policy checks). In Kubernetes, shared clusters need cost allocation by namespace and label (OpenCost, Kubecost, or the providers' split cost allocation).
- **Visibility**: per-team dashboards and budgets with anomaly alerts (AWS Cost Anomaly Detection and similar). Showback first, chargeback if the organisation wants it.
- **Unit economics**: track cost per thousand requests, per active customer, per order or per GB processed. A bill that doubled while traffic tripled is a success; one that doubled while traffic was flat is a bug.
- **Rate optimisation** (pay less per unit) versus **usage optimisation** (use fewer units). Do usage first, then commit.

### Pricing models
- **On-demand**: flexible, most expensive.
- **Commitments**: Savings Plans or Reserved Instances (AWS), committed use discounts (Google Cloud). AWS advertises up to about 72% off on-demand for long, upfront commitments. Commit to the steady baseline you are confident about, not the peak.
- **Spot / preemptible**: spare capacity at large discounts (AWS cites up to 90%) that can be reclaimed with short notice (two minutes on AWS). Great for stateless, fault-tolerant work: CI runners, batch jobs, stateless web replicas spread across many instance types. Never for a single database primary.
- **ARM instances** often give better price-performance for workloads that support them.

## Cost traps
The bill line items that surprise people:
- **NAT gateway processing**: charged per GB on top of hourly fees. Private workloads pulling container images, calling S3 or third-party APIs through NAT add up fast. Use VPC gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) and interface endpoints for heavy AWS API traffic, and pull images through a registry in-region.
- **Cross-AZ data transfer**: charged per GB in each direction on AWS. Chatty microservices, replicas reading across zones, and Kafka replication across AZs can cost more than the compute. Topology-aware routing helps.
- **Internet egress**: serving large files directly from origin instead of through a CDN.
- **Idle and orphaned resources**: unattached EBS volumes, old snapshots, idle load balancers, forgotten test clusters, unused elastic IPs (public IPv4 addresses are billed hourly on AWS since 2024).
- **Over-provisioned requests in Kubernetes**: pods requesting 2 CPUs and using 0.2 strand capacity that nodes still pay for. Right-size from p95 usage (VPA recommendations, Goldilocks).
- **Observability volume**: verbose logs ingested at per-GB prices, high-cardinality metric labels (user IDs in labels), traces at 100% sampling. Sample, set retention, drop debug logs in production.
- **Always-on non-production**: staging and preview environments running 24/7 at production size. Scale them down at night and on weekends, use smaller instances, auto-delete previews.
- **Storage class neglect**: years of logs and backups in hot storage. Use lifecycle rules to transition and expire.
- **Serverless loops and runaway concurrency**: a recursive trigger or retry storm. Set concurrency caps and budget alerts.
- **Managed service minimums**: some managed products bill a floor per cluster or per hour even when idle.

## Investigating a cost spike
```text
1. Cost explorer: group by service, then by usage type, then by tag/account. Which line moved?
2. Correlate with time: did it start on a deploy, a traffic change, a new feature, a config change?
3. Drill into the resource: which bucket, which NAT, which cluster/namespace, which log group?
4. Fix the cause (code, config, architecture), not just the symptom.
5. Add a guardrail: budget alert, anomaly detection, policy check, dashboard, so it cannot silently recur.
```

## Trade-offs
- Aggressive scale-to-zero saves money and adds cold starts. Keep a floor for latency-critical paths.
- Commitments lower rates and reduce flexibility; over-committing on a shrinking workload wastes money.
- Spot saves a lot and adds interruption handling; mix spot with on-demand for a guaranteed floor.
- Engineering time is a cost too. Saving $200 a month with two weeks of work is a bad trade; fixing a $20,000 NAT bill with a VPC endpoint is a great one.

## In the interview
**What they probe:** whether you pick scaling signals from how the workload saturates, understand lag and headroom, can do back-of-the-envelope capacity maths, and treat cost as an engineering metric with known traps. Senior candidates should connect capacity to failure domains and cost to unit economics.

**A 60-second answer outline** for "design autoscaling for a spiky service":
1. Measure: load test to find per-pod capacity at the SLO and identify the saturating resource.
2. Signal: CPU if compute-bound, in-flight requests or queue depth if I/O-bound; KEDA for queues.
3. Behaviour: fast scale-up, slow scale-down, min replicas sized for the trough plus one AZ loss, max bounded by downstream limits and quotas.
4. Node layer: Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler, headroom for the 2-5 minute lag, scheduled pre-scaling for known peaks.
5. Safety net: rate limiting and load shedding when demand outruns capacity; cost tracked as cost per thousand requests.

**Follow-ups to expect:** Why is CPU a bad signal for this service? What happens to the database when you scale pods tenfold? How do you use spot safely? What would you look at first if the bill doubled? How do you allocate costs in a shared Kubernetes cluster?
keyPoints: Scale on the signal that tracks saturation for that workload: CPU for compute-bound services, concurrency or queue depth for I/O-bound ones.
Autoscaling has lag at every layer (metrics, pods, nodes); keep headroom, scale up fast and down slowly, and pre-scale for known peaks.
Capacity planning: find per-instance throughput at your latency SLO by load testing, apply Little's law, and size for peak plus a failure domain.
FinOps is a practice, not a tool: tag everything, make costs visible to the teams that cause them, and track unit cost such as cost per thousand requests.
Typical traps: NAT and cross-AZ data transfer, egress, idle and forgotten resources, over-provisioned requests, log and metric volume, and always-on non-production environments.

Your cloud bill doubled last month. How do you investigate and bring it down?
How do you do capacity planning for a service?

check.q: A Node.js API spends most of its time waiting on a database. CPU sits at 20% while latency climbs under load. Which autoscaling signal fits best?
options: Memory usage
CPU utilisation with a lower target
In-flight requests per pod or request latency, since CPU does not track saturation for this workload
Disk I/O
check.why: For I/O-bound services CPU stays low while the real bottleneck (concurrency, connection pools, event-loop queueing) saturates. Scale on concurrency or a request-rate metric, and check the database is not the true limit.

check.q: A service handles 2,000 requests per second with an average latency of 50 ms. By Little's law, about how many requests are in flight at once?
check.why: L = lambda x W = 2,000 per second x 0.05 seconds = 100 concurrent requests. That tells you how much concurrency your instances and connection pools must sustain.

check.q: Which change is most likely to cut a large NAT gateway bill caused by private workloads reading from S3?
options: Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint so that traffic bypasses the NAT
Move the workloads to bigger instances
Enable S3 versioning
Add a second NAT gateway
check.why: Traffic through a NAT gateway is billed per GB processed. A gateway endpoint for S3 routes that traffic privately with no NAT processing charge.

stack: Kubernetes (kind locally, or a managed cluster)
projects.summary: Take a small Node.js API from commit to production on Kubernetes: cached multi-stage image builds, scanning and signing in CI, Terraform-managed infrastructure, GitOps with Argo CD, automated canary releases gated on Prometheus metrics, autoscaling, and zero-downtime database migrations.
projects.why: Most candidates can say 'I deployed to Kubernetes'. Few can show a pipeline where a bad release is caught at 5% traffic and rolled back automatically, a schema change ships without downtime, and nothing in CI holds a long-lived cloud key. This project demonstrates the platform and reliability judgement hiring managers look for in senior backend, platform and SRE roles, with numbers you measured and a live demo of a failed canary rolling itself back.
projects.architecture:
```text
dev push -> GitHub Actions
   PR:   lint, typecheck, unit + integration tests (Postgres service), docker build (gha cache)
   main: build once -> tag :sha -> Trivy scan -> cosign sign (keyless OIDC) -> push GHCR
         -> open PR in deploy repo: bump image digest in overlays/staging

deploy repo (Kustomize: base + overlays/staging, overlays/prod)
   Argo CD (in cluster) watches -> syncs Rollout, Service, HPA, PDB, migration Job

cluster (Terraform: VPC, managed k8s or kind, node pools, OIDC roles)
   Gateway API route -> Service(stable) / Service(canary)
   Argo Rollouts: 5% -> analysis -> 25% -> analysis -> 100% (abort -> rollback)
   Prometheus scrapes app metrics (RED, by version) -> AnalysisTemplate queries
   HPA on in-flight requests; Postgres (managed or in-cluster for dev)
```
Key decisions: build once and promote the digest; pull-based GitOps so CI never holds cluster credentials; canary gated on error ratio and p99 latency compared with the stable version; migrations as a pre-sync Job using expand and contract; OIDC for all cloud access; everything reproducible from Terraform plus the deploy repo.

deepDives.title: Build once, promote by digest
deepDives.body:
The pipeline builds the image exactly once per commit and everything downstream refers to the **digest** (`ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:...`), never to a mutable tag. Staging and production differ only in Kustomize overlays (config, replica counts, resources).

Why it matters: rebuilding per environment can pull a newer base image or dependency, so the bytes in production were never tested. Tags can be moved; digests cannot. Rollback becomes 'set the previous digest', which Argo CD does from Git history.

The promotion flow is a pull request in the deploy repo that changes one line. That gives review, an audit trail and a trivially revertible change. Automation (a small script or a tool such as Argo CD Image Updater or Kargo) can open those PRs; a human or a policy merges the prod one.

deepDives.title: Canary analysis that does not cry wolf
deepDives.body:
The Rollout sends 5% of traffic to the canary, then runs an AnalysisTemplate against Prometheus every minute. Two metrics gate promotion:

- **5xx ratio** of the canary, compared with the stable version over the same window, so a downstream blip that hurts both versions does not fail the canary.
- **p99 latency** of the canary under a fixed threshold relative to stable.

```text
fail if canary_5xx_ratio > max(0.01, 2 x stable_5xx_ratio) for 2 of 5 checks
fail if canary_p99 > 1.3 x stable_p99 for 2 of 5 checks
```

Low traffic is the hard part: at 5% of a quiet service, one error swings the ratio wildly. Mitigations: require a minimum request count before evaluating, use longer windows, allow `failureLimit` of more than one, and generate synthetic traffic in staging. Every metric is labelled with the pod template hash so the queries can split by version. A failed analysis aborts the Rollout and shifts weight back to stable within one evaluation interval.

deepDives.title: Migrations as a separate, compatible step
deepDives.body:
Running migrations in every pod's startup means ten replicas race to take the same lock, and a rollback leaves code that does not match the schema. Instead, migrations run once in an Argo CD **PreSync hook Job** before the new Rollout starts, with `SET lock_timeout = '5s'` so a blocked `ALTER TABLE` fails fast instead of queuing every other query behind it.

Every migration must be compatible with both the current and the previous app version, because the canary runs both side by side and a rollback brings the old one back. Breaking changes are split with expand and contract: add the new column, dual-write, backfill in batches of a few thousand rows with sleeps, switch reads, stop writing the old column, and drop it in a later release. Indexes use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. A k6 script runs throughout to prove zero failed requests.

deepDives.title: Autoscaling from measured capacity
deepDives.body:
The HPA does not target CPU, because the API is I/O-bound: CPU sat around 25% while p99 latency crossed the SLO. A load test on a single pod found the knee at about N in-flight requests; the HPA targets 70% of that via a custom metric exposed through the Prometheus Adapter.

Scale-up is aggressive (100% every 30 seconds, no stabilisation) and scale-down cautious (300-second window, 20% per minute). `minReplicas` covers the daily trough with one zone lost; `maxReplicas` is capped by the Postgres connection budget: replicas x pool size must stay under the database's limit, with a pooler in front if that cap is too low.

The write-up records the per-pod capacity, the scale-up timeline during a k6 spike (metrics delay, pod start, node provisioning) and the resulting cost per thousand requests, which is what makes the result discussable in an interview.
